title: Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of image accessibility and troubleshooting in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with testing alternative text, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Text, links, lists, images, and media are the building blocks of readable, navigable web content; the markup should communicate meaning even before CSS is added.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Text, links, lists, images, and media are the building blocks of readable, navigable web content; the markup should communicate meaning even before CSS is added.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Write alternative text for the image’s purpose in context: describe meaningful information or function, use alt="" for decoration, and avoid repeating nearby text.

items.title: Testing alternative text
items.text: Write alternative text for the image’s purpose in context: describe meaningful information or function, use alt="" for decoration, and avoid repeating nearby text.

items.title: Identifying missing images
items.text: Identifying missing images is one of the decisions covered by Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Diagnosing incorrect file paths
items.text: Resolve the URL relative to the current document or base URL. Prefer meaningful link text, test internal paths from each page location, and verify external destinations.

items.title: Handling images that fail to load
items.text: Handling images that fail to load is one of the decisions covered by Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Testing image presentation on different screens
items.text: Use a repeatable loop: reproduce the issue, inspect the source and rendered DOM, read validator or console output, fix one cause, then retest the expected behavior.

content_blocks.expected_output: The browser displays the image if the file exists, followed by its caption. Replace the sample path with your own image.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in an .html file and open it in a modern browser. Inspect the result, then run an HTML validator if the lesson concerns syntax or structure. Example paths are illustrative; provide the referenced files or adjust paths before evaluating media/resource behavior.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the snippet in this lesson file or paste it into a fresh index.html file, then repeat the check.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Test a short page without relying on color alone: navigate with the keyboard, inspect headings/labels, and write down one improvement.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for image accessibility and troubleshooting.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The browser displays the image if the file exists, followed by its caption. Replace the sample path with your own image.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Image Accessibility and Troubleshooting is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.
Use a repeatable loop: reproduce the issue, inspect the source and rendered DOM, read validator or console output, fix one cause, then retest the expected behavior.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
